testCases.name: test_case_2
testCases.input: how did mmlu pro improve on the original mmlu?
testCases.actualOutput:
MMLU Pro was built as a direct response to the saturation that the original MMLU had reached. The creators of the new benchmark wanted to keep the spirit of a broad, multi‑disciplinary test but make it harder for models that had already been “seeing” the old questions in their training data. To do that they made a few concrete changes.

First, they trimmed the breadth of the test. The original MMLU covered 57 subjects, but MMLU Pro narrowed that down to just 12. Each of those 12 subjects now contains about 1,000 questions, so the total number of items is still large (roughly 12 k), but the focus is deeper within each discipline. By concentrating on fewer subjects, the benchmark can ask more nuanced, higher‑level questions that are less likely to be memorized from training data.

Second, they increased the difficulty of the questions themselves. While the format of having 10 answer options per question stayed the same, the new items are designed to require more reasoning and less rote recall. The creators explicitly added “reasoning” questions that push models to connect concepts rather than simply match a pattern.

Finally, MMLU Pro was marketed as “MMLU rebuilt to fix its flaws.” That tagline signals that the designers aimed to address the specific weaknesses that had been identified in the original benchmark—chief among them the fact that models were quickly reaching the ceiling of performance and that the test was no longer a good way to distinguish between newer, more capable models.

So, in short, MMLU Pro improved on the original MMLU by narrowing the subject set to 12, deepening each subject with about 1,000 harder, reasoning‑heavy questions, and keeping the 10‑option format while raising the overall difficulty to counteract saturation.

testCases.name: test_case_0
testCases.input: what is vibe testing and why isn't it enough for deploying an llm app?
testCases.actualOutput:
Vibe testing is a very informal way of checking an LLM‑based application. You simply fire off a handful of prompts—usually five or ten—read the answers, and decide by “feel” whether the system is working. If the responses seem right, you assume the app is good enough to use. It’s a quick, ad‑hoc check that relies on a single person’s intuition rather than any systematic metric.

Because it’s so casual, vibe testing has several serious shortcomings that make it unsuitable for production deployments. First, it’s subjective: different people may judge the same answers differently, so there’s no objective standard. Second, it’s not repeatable. The prompts you ask today may be different from those you ask tomorrow, and the model’s responses can drift over time, so you can’t reliably reproduce the same test conditions. Third, it only gives you a snapshot of a few scenarios; real users will ask a much wider variety of questions, and the model may fail in ways you didn’t anticipate. Finally, the lack of a formal evaluation pipeline means you miss out on automated, continuous testing that can catch regressions whenever you change the code or the model.

These limitations were highlighted by real‑world case studies—Air Canada’s chatbot, for example—where a system that passed a quick vibe test ended up hallucinating policy details and giving customers incorrect information. The lesson is that while vibe testing can be a quick sanity check during early development, it doesn’t provide the rigorous, repeatable, and objective assessment needed to safely deploy an LLM application in production. Instead, you need a structured evaluation framework, often integrated into CI/CD pipelines, that measures performance against defined metrics and only allows deployment when those metrics meet a high threshold.

testCases.name: test_case_1
testCases.actualOutput: The MMLU benchmark is a systematic test for measuring how much factual and world knowledge a large language model has learned. It was introduced in 2020 and consists of about 14,000 multiple‑choice questions spread across roughly 57 different subjects—ranging from math and science to humanities and social sciences. By asking a model to answer each question and recording the percentage of correct responses, researchers can gauge the breadth of knowledge the model has retained from its training data. Because the questions are publicly available, later models can become “contaminated” by having seen the questions during training, which eventually leads to the benchmark becoming saturated and less useful for distinguishing newer models. Nonetheless, MMLU remains a foundational benchmark for evaluating LLM knowledge.
